items.stem: An agent's trace contains these four lines. Which one could the model not have written by itself?

options.feedback: This is an Observation. It comes from the test runner. The model can write a guess about the tests, but it cannot know the result without running them.

options.text: I should confirm the tests still pass.
options.feedback: This is a Thought. The model writes its own thoughts.
This is an Action. The model writes the request. A separate program carries it out.

options.text: Done. I will also tidy the imports.
options.feedback: This is a Thought. The model decides what to do next, even when the decision is unwise.

items.stem: What makes an agent different from a chat with a language model?

options.text: It takes actions, gets results back from outside the model, and acts on them.
options.feedback: The loop of Thought, Action and Observation is the difference. A chat produces only text.

options.text: The agent uses a much larger model than the chat does.
options.feedback: Size is not the difference. The same model can run in a chat or inside an agent.

options.text: The agent remembers everything between sessions, which a chat cannot.
options.feedback: An agent sees only what fits in its context window, the same as a chat does.

options.text: The agent does not make mistakes because it checks its work.
options.feedback: It can still make mistakes, and it can act on them quickly. Checking only helps when an Observation contradicts it.

items.stem: Before you try it: the tests pass at step 15 and the task is done. What do you expect the agent to do next?

options.text: Keep going and make a change nobody asked for.
options.feedback: The model stops only when it predicts an end signal. Here it decides to tidy the imports, which adds work for you to review.
Nothing forces it to stop. Stopping is a prediction like any other output.

options.text: Ask you for permission before making more changes.
options.feedback: The agent in this trace does not ask. Approval only happens if the client is set up to require it.

items.try: Press Run it in the widget above and watch the last three steps and the two cost numbers.

items.stem: An agent has worked for 25 steps. It now ignores the formatting rule you gave in your first message. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The first message has left the context window, so the rule is no longer visible.
options.feedback: Every thought, action and observation is added to the context. When it fills, the oldest text, which includes your first instruction, is no longer visible.

options.text: The model got tired after so many steps and stopped paying attention.
options.feedback: A model does not tire. Its behavior changes only because of what is in its context.

options.text: The tests failed, so the agent stopped following instructions.
options.feedback: A failed test is one more Observation. It does not cancel your instructions.

options.text: The model never read the first message in the first place.
options.feedback: It read it at the start. The problem is that the message is no longer in view.

items.stem: At step 3 an agent reads a file and misunderstands what it does. What is most likely to happen over steps 4 to 20?

options.text: It treats the mistake as fact and builds on it until an Observation contradicts it.
options.feedback: Errors compound. The model's confidence does not fade, and only a result from outside the model can correct it.

options.text: It notices the mistake by itself within a step or two and corrects it.
options.feedback: Nothing in the loop checks the reading. The model has no outside source for that check.

options.text: Only step 4 is affected, because each later step starts fresh.
options.feedback: Each later step uses everything before it, so one wrong belief can shape many steps.

options.text: It stops as soon as it makes any error, since errors end the loop.
options.feedback: The loop has no rule that stops on errors. It stops when the model predicts an end signal.
